e01:
You don’t need land yet. The small group that’s still deciding whether to build a community already is the first community. Even if it’s just three people around somebody’s kitchen table, that counts.

Don’t combine ownership and major resources without going through at least one real conflict together, start to finish. Not writing a vision statement and shaking hands on it, or settling for a truce nobody believes. I mean actually going through the conflict together, emotionally. That’s relational pl/ork. Somebody names what happened, and each person gets time. You find out which jealousy, humiliation, fear or old material is involved, and you only reach an agreement once the emotional pressure has changed enough for it to mean something.
e02: Whoever owns the land has enormous power over the community. If the deed is in the founder’s name, the founder is basically a landlord with a philosophy. And if three members out of twelve own everything? Then you have two classes of members, whatever the welcome packet says about everyone being equal.
e03: Even a money-free community has scarce things and bottlenecks, so the material side has to be visible to everyone. Members ought to be able to see what the community owns or holds in common and what’s been set aside, and what it owes to anyone outside. They should be able to find out who can hand out major resources, and where the conflicts of interest are. Big transfers of land, equipment, stored supplies or outside cash shouldn’t depend on one person’s memory or say-so. Define exit rights, too, so people can leave with something, in whatever form makes sense: cash if the community uses it, and also tools, transport, temporary housing, stored goods or the right to keep using something. Otherwise the right to leave is a paper right that only works when the community happens to have spare money. That’s not much of a right.
e04: Good people leave for good reasons, like a dying parent, love or work. Health and exhaustion count too, and so does a changed mind. If leaving means giving up everything they put in, staying becomes coercive. Exit terms are best written while nobody is leaving and it’s all still hypothetical. It’s the community version of a prenup that you work out while planning the wedding. Nobody finds that romantic, but it protects people. And it’s much easier to do before anybody is furious. If you want the whole sequence, Diana Leafe Christian’s Creating a Life Together has it: the vision first, then the members, then pooling major resources, and the land last.
e05:
Correspond first. Have they read the materials? Do they understand why the community exists, and have they started the relevant practices? A thoughtful back-and-forth costs so much less than six months of misunderstanding!

Short visit: a week or two of daily life with the group. Most people can be charming for two weeks, so congrats, you’ve found out they can be charming for two weeks. 😅
e06: Long visit: stay long enough for the inconvenience and the conflicts to show up. Watch how the person reacts when they’re tired or corrected, attracted or disappointed, or just bored. Even a professional faker can sometimes keep it up for months! So time gets you more evidence, not certainty.
e07: Provisional membership: decide how long it lasts and what rights and responsibilities come with it, plus how the review works and how they’d leave. Who decides whether they move on to full membership? Not the person who recruited them. Then full membership: rights to the land and shared resources, a voice, and long-term obligations, as your founding agreements set them out.
e08:
At each stage, judge people by their conduct, however spiritual or therapeutic they sound. Going by vibes is so easy! So is mistaking conformity for safety. Six months gives you a bigger sample, but it won’t tell you who’s a good person.

If someone’s going to have a role with real consequences, around children, shared resources, medicine, vehicles or private records, you want evidence of how they handle that specific thing. Have you seen them do it? Use references where they make sense and give access in stages. There should also be an independent way to challenge the decision.
e09: Before anyone becomes a provisional member, do more than hang out together. Can the group decide things and work together, or does it only get along? Make one real group decision, do one ordinary work or shared-resource task, and process one small conflict afterward. A trial run like that won’t show you anyone’s soul, but it can show you whether your way of coordinating works before anybody sells a house.
e10: Visitors, volunteers, workers, renters and interns don’t need full political membership to have rights. If a decision really affects their pay or their access to shared resources, they need clear terms and a way to be heard, and the decision should be open to review. The same goes for decisions that really affect their schedule, safety, housing, records or discipline. Equality that stops at the membership line? That can bring back a servant class of non-members moving between communes.
e11: A safe community can’t promise to keep everyone. And if somebody is a serious or general danger, keeps violating essential boundaries, or has become impossible to live with? Then ejecting them can be the right answer. Restorative work is useful if it can work in a reasonable amount of time. If someone is endangering everyone else, though, nobody has a duty to turn the commune into their treatment program.
e12: But the power to remove somebody is also one of the easiest powers to abuse! So work out the process before it's about anyone in particular. The process should say what kind of conduct calls for protective action right away, and who preserves the evidence. Anyone who’s too close to the case steps aside, and it should be clear who decides on temporary restrictions. The person gets a way to reply, and some kind of review or appeal that doesn’t put others in danger. While they’re separated, their housing, records and contact with family need protecting, and so does their access to common resources, or to outside funds if there are any. The process should also say when to call for outside help.
e13: “Outside” doesn’t always mean the nation-state. I’ll admit my research leaned too far that way at first. What matters is a competent layer that isn’t reviewing its own conduct. That could be another community, a federation or a professional. It could be an autonomous regional institution, or a court, a regulator or an emergency service. The Zapatistas are an important correction here: autonomous institutions can review local power without becoming the state. But autonomy doesn’t give anyone permission to erase individual rights that can’t be waived, and it doesn’t make outside jurisdiction disappear.
e14: Also pick a mediator or ombud before there’s a crisis. Why ahead of time? Because people who meet the “neutral stranger” for the first time on the day things explode often don’t trust them. Mediation is there to repair things, but it doesn’t replace evidence, safeguarding or a ruling, and once someone no longer consents to living together, it can’t stand in for a final separation.
